person.name: Ida_Noddack
person.summary: German chemist and physicist who, working closely with Walter Noddack and Otto Berg, reported the discovery of rhenium and later publicly challenged interpretations of neutron-bombarded uranium by proposing that heavy nuclei could break into large fragments.

portrait.caption: Stylized portrait based on historical photograph
portrait.creator: AI generated artwork

conclusion: Ida Noddack built a scientific life on meticulous analysis and intellectual nerve—moving from industrial chemistry into element hunting, public acclaim, and sharp dissent. Co-discoverer of rhenium and an early voice pointing toward nuclear fission, she left a legacy defined by careful evidence and the courage to say what others were not ready to hear.

events.title: Born in Lackhausen (Lower Rhine)
events.description: Ida Tacke was born on 25 February 1896 in Lackhausen, in the northern Rhine region. She grew up in a family linked to small-scale industry through her father's varnish factory, which brought practical chemistry and materials close to everyday life.

events.title: Enters Technische Hochschule Charlottenburg
events.description: In 1915, Noddack enrolled at the [[Technische Hochschule Charlottenburg|Technische Hochschule Charlottenburg]] in Berlin. Women had only recently been admitted to study across Berlin’s universities, and she chose the school for its long, demanding chemistry program.

Technische Hochschule Charlottenburg.explanation: The former name of what later became the Technical University of Berlin (Technische Universität Berlin), a major German engineering and science university.

events.title: Graduated in chemical engineering
events.description: In 1918, she graduated with a degree in chemical and metallurgical engineering. Her research work focused on higher [[aliphatic|aliphatic]] fatty-acid anhydrides.

aliphatic.explanation: In organic chemistry, aliphatic compounds are non-aromatic hydrocarbons (straight-chain, branched, or non-aromatic cyclic), a broad class that includes many fatty-acid derivatives.

events.date_note: End date approximates the period up to her doctoral dissertation publication
events.title: Worked at AEG laboratory
events.description: In 1918, after completing her studies, Noddack took a position in the chemistry laboratory of [[AEG|AEG’s]] turbine works in Berlin, doing analytical work inside a large industrial manufacturing environment. The turbine-hall building itself—designed by Peter Behrens—was already world-famous, a daily reminder that chemistry could be both exacting and monumental.

AEG.explanation: Allgemeine Elektricitäts-Gesellschaft (AEG), a major German electrical engineering and manufacturing company with large industrial plants in Berlin.

events.title: Published doctoral dissertation
events.description: In 1921, she issued her doctoral dissertation in Germany, marking the formal completion of her university training and her entry into professional chemical research.

events.date_note: The main article places the element search at the Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt in the period leading up to the 1925 publication
events.title: Began element search program
events.description: In 1922, while working at the [[Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt|Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt (PTR)]], she joined Walter Noddack and Otto Berg in a coordinated search for the then-unknown elements 43 and 75, analyzing mineral samples for evidence of new elements.

Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt.explanation: Germany’s national institute for science and measurement (metrology), based in Berlin at the time, where precision physical and chemical research was carried out.

events.title: Reports rhenium; claims “masurium”
events.description: In 1925, Noddack and her co-authors reported evidence for element 75—proposing the name rhenium—and also claimed evidence for element 43, for which they suggested the name [[masurium|masurium]]. They defended their methods as other chemists questioned whether element 43 had really been detected.

masurium.explanation: A name proposed in 1925 by the Noddacks and Otto Berg for the then-unconfirmed element 43 (now known as technetium); the name referred to Masuria (German: Masuren) in East Prussia.

event_class.title: Zwei neue Elemente der Mangangruppe, Chemischer Teil
event_class.impact: The paper presented the group’s chemical case for two missing periodic-table elements and set off attempts to replicate and verify their results.

events.title: Married Walter Noddack
events.description: In 1926, she married Walter Noddack after several years of close scientific collaboration, establishing a shared household while continuing their joint research partnership.

events.title: Isolated rhenium sample
events.description: In 1928, Ida Noddack and her collaborators intensified their work to isolate rhenium by processing large quantities of [[molybdenite|molybdenite]]. Through painstaking separations and repeated checks, they aimed to show—under scrutiny—that the element could be obtained as a tangible sample, not just a calculation on paper.

molybdenite.explanation: A molybdenum sulfide mineral (MoS₂) that can contain trace amounts of rhenium, making it an important source material for rhenium extraction.

location_coordinates.label: Berlin
location_coordinates.name: Berlin, Germany

events.title: Received Liebig Medal
events.description: In 1931, Ida Noddack received the [[Liebig Medal|Liebig Medal]] from the [[German Chemical Society|German Chemical Society]] for her analytical contributions connected to the rhenium and “masurium” investigations, a distinction that affirmed her standing in German chemistry.

Liebig Medal.explanation: An award of the German Chemical Society (GDCh), named after chemist Justus von Liebig, recognizing outstanding achievements in chemistry.

German Chemical Society.explanation: Germany’s main professional society for chemists (today the Gesellschaft Deutscher Chemiker, GDCh), which awards major national chemistry honors.

events.date_note: Nominations occurred in multiple separate years; represented here as a single span
events.title: Nominated three times for Nobel Prize
events.description: In Germany in the early 1930s, Ida Noddack and Walter Noddack were nominated three times for the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. As employment rules for married women tightened—especially after 1933 under [[Nazi Germany]]—she continued participating in their research partly in the informal role of an “unpaid collaborator.”

Nazi Germany.explanation: The German state under National Socialist rule (1933–1945); policies introduced soon after 1933 increasingly restricted many groups, including married women, in parts of public employment.

events.title: Published Das Rhenium
events.description: In 1933, Ida Noddack and Walter Noddack issued their monograph on rhenium as a follow-up to their earlier work on the element, aiming to give chemists and physicists a single reference point for the emerging literature.

events.title: Publishes “On Element 93” critique
events.description:
In 1934, Enrico Fermi bombarded uranium with neutrons and argued the new radioactivity he observed was evidence of a [[transuranic element|transuranic]] element. Ida Noddack responded quickly in her paper “On Element 93,” challenging the logic of that conclusion.

Her criticism wasn’t that Fermi’s results were imaginary, but that his chemical eliminations were incomplete: she argued that ruling out only the heaviest neighboring elements was not enough, because lighter products might be hiding in the chemistry. Then she pressed a further possibility—briefly, almost daringly—that the nucleus itself might break up into several large fragments, producing isotopes of known elements rather than a new element just beyond uranium.

Today that sentence is read as an early, public hint of what would later be called [[nuclear fission]]. At the time, it landed without the kind of experimental proof or theoretical framework her peers demanded. The idea was widely ignored and mocked; several German scientists, including [[Otto Hahn]], dismissed it as “ridiculous.”

transuranic element.explanation: A chemical element with an atomic number greater than uranium (92). Early neutron experiments sometimes appeared to create such elements before fission was understood.

nuclear fission.explanation: A nuclear reaction in which a heavy nucleus splits into lighter nuclei, releasing energy and additional neutrons; formally established in 1938–1939.

Otto Hahn.explanation: German radiochemist; later central to the experimental chain leading to fission’s establishment, and among those who dismissed Noddack’s 1934 suggestion.

event_class.title: Über das Element 93
event_class.impact: The paper publicly pressed for alternative chemical interpretations of neutron-irradiation products and proposed a fragmentation possibility for heavy nuclei.

events.title: Wins Scheele Medal, secures patent
events.description: In 1934, Ida Noddack and Walter Noddack received the [[Scheele Medal|Scheele Medal of the Swedish Chemical Society]]. In the same year, they also secured a German patent connected to their rhenium-related work, linking their laboratory research to a protected industrial process.

images.caption: Framsida av medalj med Karl Vilhelm Scheele i profil
images.creator: Gustaf Adolf Enegren

Scheele Medal.explanation: An award of the Swedish Chemical Society, named after chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele, given in recognition of notable contributions to chemistry.

event_class.title: Rhenium concentrate process
event_class.description: A patented chemical process for producing a rhenium-rich concentrate from mineral sources through targeted separation and concentration steps.
event_class.impact: It formalized a practical route to enriched rhenium material for further laboratory and industrial handling.

events.title: Widowed by Walter's death
events.description: [[Walter Noddack|Walter Noddack]] died on 7 December 1960, ending his long domestic and scientific partnership with Ida Noddack.

events.title: Death in Germany
events.description: Ida Noddack died in [[Bad Neuenahr|Bad Neuenahr]] (West Germany) on 24 September 1978, aged 82.

Bad Neuenahr.explanation: A spa town (now part of Bad Neuenahr-Ahrweiler) in Rhineland-Palatinate, then in West Germany, reported as Noddack's place of death.
